content.title: About
content.content: Black tea is a drink made from fully oxidized (fermented) leaves of the tea plant Camellia sinensis. It has a rich, slightly astringent flavor, a dark brew, and a deep aroma. Black tea is drunk hot or iced, with milk, lemon, sugar, or honey, and is also used in blends with spices and flavorings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black and green tea are made from the leaves of the same plant, Camellia sinensis; the difference is in the processing.
Well-known black tea varieties include Assam, Darjeeling, Ceylon, and Keemun.
Earl Grey tea is flavored with bergamot oil.
In China, black tea is called red tea because of the color of the brew.
Black tea is the most popular type of tea in the world.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Theaflavins and other polyphenols in black tea have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains caffeine
items.content: Caffeine supports alertness and concentration; a cup of tea usually has less than a cup of coffee.

items.title: Contains L-theanine
items.content: This amino acid works together with caffeine and may promote calm focus.

items.title: May be part of a heart-friendly diet
items.content: In observational studies, moderate tea drinking is linked to heart and vascular health.

items.title: Calorie-free
items.content: Tea without sugar or milk adds practically no calories and helps you keep up your fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: In large amounts, the caffeine in tea can cause anxiety, insomnia, and a racing heartbeat.

items.title: Reduced iron absorption
items.content: Tannins in tea can reduce the absorption of iron from plant foods, so people with low iron should drink tea between meals.

items.title: Very hot tea
items.content: Regularly drinking very hot beverages is linked to a higher risk of esophageal problems; let tea cool a little first.

items.title: Teeth and additions
items.content: Tea can stain tooth enamel, and sugar and syrups add calories and harm teeth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use about a teaspoon of leaves per cup, pour over freshly boiled water, and steep for 3–5 minutes. Over-steeped tea turns bitter. Drink it with milk, lemon, honey, or sugar, or chill the brew for iced tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry tea in an airtight container in a dry, dark, cool place away from strong-smelling foods. The aroma fades over time, so use tea within a reasonable period. Keep brewed tea in the refrigerator for no more than a day.
